Chromosome 1 is incorrect. The gene for variegate porphyria (the PPOX gene) has been located to chromosome 1. It has an autosomal-dominant pattern of inheritance.

Chromosome 6
Chromosome 6 is incorrect. Hereditary haemochromatosis is an autosomal-recessive disorder with variable penetrance, and results from a mutation of the HFE gene located on chromosome 6. This encodes a transport protein found in the duodenum. 77.5% of patients have two copies of the C282Y mutation, 4% have one copy, while 6.5% have one or two copies of a different mutation, H63D.

Chromosome 7
Chromosome 7 is incorrect. Cystic fibrosis is caused by a mutation of the CFTR gene, which is normally found on chromosome 7.

Chromosome.

stem: You are reviewing pre-clinical data on a new agent thought to decrease foam cell activity and plaque stability. Which of the following correctly describes the lineage of the majority of foam cells?
explanation:
Monocytes
A number of studies have attempted to define the lineage of foam cells. A large percentage of these cells are CD68-positive, which indicates a monocyte lineage. Other foam-like cells appear to be derived from smooth muscle cells; these contain extensive lipid inclusion bodies and stain positive for smooth muscle cell proteins such as actin, vimentin and desmin. Finally some cells expressing the foam cell phenotype that stain for S-100 are also found. S-100 is a protein expressed by vascular dendritic cells.

stem: You are asked to see a patient who had a chest drain removed 4 days ago. There appears to be some infection around the chest drain site. Which one of the following statements regarding stages in the cell biology of normal wound healing is true?
options: Acute inflammation usually lasts for 6–12 hours
Collagen deposition is the key process during demolition
Epithelial cell proliferation is the hallmark of the demolition phase
Maturation and remodelling can continue for up to a year
explanation:
Maturation and remodelling can continue for up to a year
Maturation and remodeling of a wound lasts for up to 12 months, during which time the tensile strength of the wound increases and the random collagen is replaced by a more stable form orientated along lines of stress.

Acute inflammation usually lasts for 6–12 hours
Acute inflammation usually lasts for 6–12 hours is incorrect. The first phase in healing by first intention is the phase of acute inflammation that lasts up to 3 days, if uncomplicated: The initiating factor appears to originate from platelets activated by mature collagen exposed in the wound. Platelets first aggregate then release a variety of active agents including lysosomal enzymes, ATP, serotonin and wound cytokines. A fibrin clot develops, which completes haemostasis and provides strength and support towith the AI wound. The surface dries to form a scab. Platelets and macrophage factors cause local vasodilatation, which produces warmth and increases capillary permeability, allowing serum and white blood cells to accumulate and cause swelling.

Collagen deposition is the key process during demolition
Collagen deposition is the key process during demolition is incorrect. After the initial acute inflammation, macrophages become active as the main agents of demolition, removing unwanted fibrin, dead cells and bacteria and creating fluid-filled spaces for granulation tissue. Macrophages also release factors that stimulate the formation of new capillary buds during this phase, and later they initiate and control fibroblast activity during repair. Within the connective tissue, randomly orientated collagen begins to form after a few days, reaching a peak of activity after 5–7 days.

Demolition is the first phase
Demolition is the first phase is incorrect. Acute inflammation that is the first phase of wound healing.

Epithelial cell proliferation is the hallmark of the demolition phase
Epithelial cell proliferation is the hallmark of the demolition phase is incorrect. Epithelial cells at the edge of the wound start to proliferate after 24 hours and this phase can last for up to 3 weeks, although it is macrophage proliferation which is the hallmark of the demolition phase. You are monitoring a man who has undergone a Whipple’s procedure for pancreatic carcinoma for signs of recurrence.

stem: You are teaching molecular biology to a group of medical students, and one asks you about how reverse transcriptase works. Which one of the statements below explains how reverse transcriptase works?
options: It cleaves specific portions of DNA
It is involved in protein synthesis
explanation:
It transcribes DNA from RNA
Reverse transcriptase is a DNA polymerase enzyme that is involved in transcribing single-stranded portions of RNA into lengths of double-stranded DNA. Reverse transcriptase has an important role to play in the pathogenesis of RNA viruses, such as HIV, allowing their genetic code to be integrated into the host genome as DNA. It is also very important in molecular biology, allowing segments of DNA to be produced from messenger RNA.

It amplifies segments of DNA
It amplifies segments of DNA with It amplifies segments of DNA is incorrect. PCR is the technique used to amplify segments ofChat DNA.

It cleaves specific portions of DNA
It cleaves specific portions of DNA is incorrect. CRISPR/cas9 is the standard technique used for genome editing with removal of specific portions of DNA.

It is involved in protein synthesis
It is involved in protein synthesis is incorrect. Because reverse transcriptase is involved in transcribing DNA from RNA, it is not involved in protein synthesis, but instead is involved in incorporation of viral genetic code into host DNA. You are considering using a TNF-α antagonist in the treatment of a 45-year-old man with severe psoriasis. The patient wants to know more about this treatment and how it works. Which cells are mainly responsible for production of TNF-α?

It transcribes RNA from DNA
It transcribes RNA from DNA is incorrect. RNA polymerase transcribes RNA from DNA and is involved in protein synthesis.

stem: You are examining a possible new treatment for solid tumours which is thought to exert its effect by pushing tumour cells into a state of cellular senescence. Which of the following defines that a cell has reached senescence?
explanation:
Arrest of mitosis
Senescence was first described in the 1960s, when a theoretical maximum of around 50 cell divisions was proposed, and that cells which escape this maximum become cancerous. It is thought to occur not just because of DNA damage at telomeric sites (shortening occurs with each cell division), but also due to DNA damage at non-telomeric sites. This leads to a DNA damage response. Cultural stress also occurs when division is attempted in vitro, but the equivalent of this cultural stress in vivo is not well described.

Apoptosis
Apoptosis with by Apoptosis is incorrect. Apoptosis is programmed cell death and can occur via the intrinsic Chat pathway (driven mitochondrial dysfunction) or by the extrinsic pathway through cell receptor mediated cell death.

Arrest of meiosis
Arrest of meiosis is incorrect. Meiosis is required for sexual reproduction, and arrest of meiosis is not a marker of senescence.

Cellular necrosis
Cellular necrosis is incorrect. Cellular necrosis occurs due to autolysis and is a marker of premature cell death rather than sensescence.

Shortening of telomeres
Shortening of telomeres is incorrect. Progressive shortening of telomeres is thought to be one mechanism underlying sensescence, but does not define senescence itself. You are asked to take part in a study of embryonic islet stem cells, which are about to be studied in humans for the first time. These cells are packaged in a membrane which allows hormones and nutrients in and out, but prevents either stem cells from passing out of the device, or immune cells from moving into the device.

stem: Most cancer cells activate telomerase. Which one of the following is the most likely biological result of this activation?
explanation:
Immortalisation
Telomeres are structures at the end of chromosomes, which in normal cells progressively shorten with each cell division. When telomerase is inactive, shortened telomeres cause cell growth arrest. Physiological suppression of telomerase is a tumour-suppressor and normal ageing mechanism. In contrast, most cancer cells pathologically activate telomerase, resulting in stable telomeres and immortalisation. Normal stem cells may express telomerase in the adult, allowing perpetuation, while tumours arising from stem cells may have a similar prolongation of survival. Telomerase inhibition is a therapeutic target to force cell senescence.

Angiogenesis
Angiogenesis is incorrect. Angiogenesis is stimulated by tumours through mechanisms such as the upregulation of vascular endothelial growth factor receptors.

Cell death Cell death is incorrect. Cancer cells are characterised by aberrations causing prolonged and uncontrolled growth and proliferation, and the avoidance of physiological cell death and tumour suppressive mechanisms.

Major histocompatibility complex activation
Major histocompatibility complex (MHC) activation is incorrect. MHC is a cell surface protein activated by the presentation of specific antigens.

Tumour suppression.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with difficulty climbing the stairs due to pain and cramping in both lower limbs, and intermittent coughing when he eats too quickly. Apparently, his maternal grandfather suffered from a similar problem and died in his mid-sixties of progressive muscle weakness and disability. No females in the family have been affected by the condition. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Kennedy disease
Kennedy disease, also known as “X-linked bulbospinal neuronopathy”, is a trinucleotide-repeat disorder.Other trinucleotide-repeat disorders include Huntington’s chorea, fragile-X syndrome, myotonic dystrophy and Friedreich’s ataxia. The typical age of onset is 40–60 years, but with repeat expansion it can appear as early as the 20s. The fact that no females have been affected by the condition drives us towards thinking about an Xlinked disorder, and the gradual onset of limb and bulbar muscle weakness points us towards Kennedy’s.

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is incorrect. This is a form of motor neurone disease where both upper and lower motor tracts are affected. Both upper and lower motor neurone signs are seen. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis may follow an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, hence male and female members of the family would be affected.

Becker’s muscular dystrophy
Becker’s muscular dystrophy is incorrect. This presents at an earlier age with predominant lower limb weakness and pseudohypertrophy of the calves.

Sydenham’s chorea
Sydenham’s chorea is incorrect. It is sometimes seen in patients with rheumatic fever and is also known as St Vitus’ dance. It is associated with choreaform movements rather than the features seen here.

Wallenberg’s syndrome.

stem: You are prescribing botulinum toxin for injection via endoscopy for the treatment of achalasia. Which of the following is true of the intervention?
options: The effect usually wears off after 4 weeks
The maximum recommended dose can be exceeded by up to 75%
The toxin is produced from the type G neurotoxin
The toxin prevents the release of acetylcholine
explanation:
The toxin prevents the release of acetylcholine
Botulinum toxin blocks cholinergic transport at the neuromuscular junction by preventing the release of acetylcholine.

The effect usually wears off after 4 weeks
The effect usually wears off after 4 weeks is incorrect. The effect of botulinum toxin is usually seen for 12 weeks or more.

The maximum recommended dose can be exceeded by up to 75%
The maximum recommended dose can be exceeded by up to 75% is incorrect. The maximum recommended dose should not be exceeded because of the risk of systemic absorption and significant (and rarely fatal) neuromuscular blockade.

The toxin is not immunogenic
The toxin is not immunogenic is incorrect. Hypersensitivity reactions are seen in association with botulinum toxin administraton, and given it is a bacterial peptide this is hardly surprising.

The toxin is produced from the type G neurotoxin.

stem: You are asked to assess a new agent which is thought to have positive effects in reducing the early asthma response (EAR). Which of the following is a characteristic of the EAR?
options: Attraction of phagocytes is a predominant feature
It occurs between 3 and 5 hours after an initial response to an allergen
It usually resolves spontaneously after 6–8 hours
Mast cell degranulation is seen in response to IgE already produced by B cells
explanation:
Mast cell degranulation is seen in response to IgE already produced by B cells
Initial exposure to the antigen stimulates B cells to produce IgE antibodies, which bind antigens and become attached to the surface of mast cells by high-affinity FceRI receptors.

Attraction of phagocytes is a predominant feature
Attraction of phagocytes is a predominant feature is incorrect. This is an important feature of the late asthma, not EAR.

Eosinophils are particularly important
Eosinophils are particularly important is incorrect. Eosinophils are a prominent component of the late asthma response, potentiating inflammation; they are recruited in response to IL-13 produced by lymphocytes.

It occurs between 3 and 5 hours after an initial response to an allergen
It occurs between 3 and 5 hours after an initial response to an allergen is incorrect. The late asthma response (LAR) occurs between 3 and 5 hours after an initial response to an allergen, and resolves spontaneously after 6–8 hours.

It usually resolves spontaneously after 6–8 hours.

stem: You are studying the effects of tetanus toxin on acetylcholine-mediated transmission at the motor endplate. Which of the following fits best with the effect of tetanus toxin?
options: A tetanus toxin fusion complex is formed which is made of synaptobrevin, syntaxin and
Tetanus toxin cleaves specific sites of SNAP-25
Tetanus toxin cleaves specific sites of synaptobrevin (VAMP)
Tetanus toxin forms a SNAP complex, together with NSF, Ca2+ and other proteins
explanation:
Tetanus toxin cleaves specific sites of synaptobrevin (VAMP)
The synaptic fusion complex is made up of synaptobrevin, syntaxin and synaptosome-associated protein (SNAP-25). The fusion complex serves to join the membranes of an acetylcholine vesicle and a nerve cell. Botulinum toxin types BoNT/B, D, F, G and tetanus toxin (TeNT) cleave specific sites of synaptobrevin (VAMP).

A tetanus toxin fusion complex is formed which is made of synaptobrevin, syntaxin and
A tetanus toxin fusion complex is formed which is made of synaptobrevin, syntaxin and synaptosome-associated protein A tetanus toxin fusion complex is formed which is made of synaptobrevin, syntaxin and synaptosomeassociated protein is incorrect. It is the synaptic fusion complex that is made up of synaptobrevin, syntaxin and synaptosome-associated protein (SNAP-25).

Tetanus toxin cleaves specific sites of SNAP-25
Tetanus toxin cleaves specific sites of SNAP-25 is incorrect. Botulinum toxin type A (BoNT/A) and E (BoNT/E) cleave specific sites of SNAP-25 (e.g. BoNT/A recognises Glu–Ala–Asn–Gln).

Tetanus toxin cleaves syntaxin
Tetanus toxin cleaves syntaxin is incorrect. Botulinum toxin type C (BoNT/C) cleaves syntaxin.

Tetanus toxin forms a SNAP complex, together with NSF, Ca2+ and other proteins.

stem: A 42-year-old man is put on a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) to suppress symptoms of oesophagitis. Which of the following is true of the mode of action of a PPI?
options: Acetylcholine-stimulated acid production overrides proton pump inhibition
Histamine-stimulated acid production overrides proton pump inhibition
PPIs are known to promote magnesium retention
Renal impairment does not necessitate dose reduction
Use with an H2 antagonist in combination significantly enhances efficacy
explanation:
Renal impairment does not necessitate dose reduction
The pharmacokinetics of proton pump inhibitors are not affected by reduced renal function.

Acetylcholine-stimulated acid production overrides proton pump inhibition
Acetylcholine-stimulated acid production overrides proton pump inhibition is incorrect. The proton pump is the final common pathway of histamine- and acetylcholine-stimulated production and PPIs are therefore not overridden by acetylcholine-stimulated acid production.

Histamine-stimulated acid production overrides proton pump inhibition
Histamine-stimulated acid production overrides proton pump inhibition is incorrect. Because the proton pump is the final common pathway for acid production, PPI effectiveness is not overridden by histamine stimulation.

PPIs are known to promote magnesium retention
PPIs are known to promote magnesium retention is incorrect. PPIs may actually promote magnesium loss, which may become symptomatic where PPIs are co-prescribed with diuretics which also promote magnesium excretion.

Use with an H2 antagonist in combination significantly enhances efficacy.

stem: You are monitoring a man who has undergone a Whipple’s procedure for pancreatic carcinoma for signs of recurrence. Which of the following is the most useful tumour marker?
explanation:
CA 19-9
CA 19-9 is a tumour surface marker, particularly associated with pancreatic cancer. It has a high false-positive rate in normal individuals without cancer, therefore it is less useful as a primary investigation and more useful to monitor for recurrence in patients with elevated levels at diagnosis.

Alpha-fetoprotein
Alpha-fetoprotein is incorrect. AFP is associated with hepatocellular carcinoma, hepatoblastoma, testicular teratoma and yolk sac tumours. A rapid increase in AFP can be seen in patients with cirrhosis who subsequently develop a hepatocellular carcinoma.

CA-125
CA-125 is incorrect. This is associated with ovarian epithelial cancers and can be considered as part of screening work-up.

CEA
CEA is incorrect. This is associated with colon cancer, and some head and neck and lung cancers.

HCG.

stem: You are investigating periodic episodes of unexplained hypoglycaemia in a 23-year-old nurse and request a Cpeptide assay. Which of the following statements fits best with the characteristics of C-peptide?
options: C-peptide cleavage is an example of post-transcriptional modification
C-peptide cleavage is an example of post-translational modification
C-peptide is attached to only the alpha chain
The level of C-peptide will be reduced in insulinoma
The level of C-peptide will be unchanged in factitious hypoglycaemia
explanation:
C-peptide cleavage is an example of post-translational modification
Pro-insulin is cleaved after manufacture to produce insulin and C-peptide, hence the modification occurs after translation of mRNA into protein.

C-peptide cleavage is an example of post-transcriptional modification
C-peptide cleavage is an example of post-transcriptional modification is incorrect. Post-transcriptional modification occurs to mRNA, e.g. RNA splicing.

C-peptide is attached to only the alpha chain
C-peptide is attached to only the alpha chain is incorrect. The C-peptide is attached to both the alpha and beta insulin chains, and cleavage of C-peptide from pro-insulin leaves free insulin formed of a linked alpha and beta chain.

The level of C-peptide will be reduced in insulinoma
The level of C-peptide will be reduced in insulinoma is incorrect. An insulinoma leads to increased levels of endogenous insulin. Therefore, C-peptide is elevated because the insulin is produced first as pro-insulin.

The level of C-peptide will be unchanged in factitious hypoglycaemia.

stem: A 22-year-old marathon runner is preparing for a special event in 3 months’ time and gradually increases his level of physical exercise. Which of the following biochemical processes is likely to contribute most to energy creation in his longdistance running?
explanation:
Fatty acid oxidation
Long-chain fatty acids and ketone bodies can only be metabolised aerobically, and their catabolism takes place exclusively in the mitochondria. Two-carbon fragments are successively removed from long-chain fatty acids (as long-chain fatty acid coenzyme A (CoA)) in a series of reactions known generically as beta-oxidation, to form acetyl-CoA. Each turn of beta-oxidation generates sufficient reducing equivalents to regenerate five ATP molecules. Acetyl-CoA is then oxidised through the tricarboxylic acid cycle to regenerate more ATP, hence the energy yield from long-chain fatty acid oxidation is considerable. Lipid-derived fuels are preferentially used by the heart, and their utilisation diminishes the use of carbohydrate, thereby conserving glucose for tissues that are obligatorily dependent on carbohydrate as an energy source.

Creatine
Creatine is incorrect. Creatine has been used as a food supplement, and may have minor effects on short-term athletic (high intensity) performance.

Glycogenesis
Glycogenesis is incorrect. Glycogen provides an initial source of energy during a long-distance run, although it is fatty acid oxidation which is most important as an energy source later in the run.

Ketogenesis
Ketogenesis is incorrect. Although ketone bodies do contribute as an energy source during endurance exercise, they are less important versus long chain fatty acids.

Lactate formation.

stem: A 54-year-old alcoholic comes to the clinic for review. He has been tired for some time and is found to be deficient in multiple B vitamins, including riboflavin. For what metabolic process is riboflavin required?
options: Synthesis of glycogen from glucose phosphate
The hydrogen-transfer chain in the mitochondria
explanation:
The hydrogen-transfer chain in the mitochondria
Riboflavin is a substituted alloxazine ring linked to ribitol, an alcohol derived from the pentose sugar ribose. Dietary sources are liver, milk, cheese, eggs, some green vegetables and beer, other sources include yeast extracts (for example, Marmite) and meat extracts (for example, Bovril). Riboflavin is involved in redox processes involving the hydrogen-transfer chain in the mitochondria and the production of ATP, there is no specific storage tissue for riboflavin.

Prostaglandin synthesis
Prostaglandin synthesis is incorrect. Vitamin D is known to modulate prostaglandin E2 synthesis.

Synthesis of glycogen from glucose phosphate
Synthesis of glycogen from glucose phosphate is incorrect. Vitamin B6 is required coenzyme of glycogen phosphorylase, the enzyme which drives glycogenolysis.

Synthesis of non-essential amino acids
Synthesis of non-essential amino acids is incorrect. Folic acid is a key requirement for amino acid synthesis.

Synthesis of the protein collagen.

stem: A family come to the Genetics Clinic with their child who has Tay–Sachs disease wishing to know some more about the condition. The accumulation of G M2 ganglioside in the central nervous system of individuals with Tay–Sachs disease is attributed to which of the following?
options: Increased permeability of the blood–brain barrier
Increase synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum
explanation:
Decreased lysosomal hydrolysis
Tay–Sachs disease is a fatal genetic lipid-storage disorder in which harmful quantities of a fatty substance called ganglioside G M2 build up in tissues and nerve cells in the brain.The condition is caused by insufficient activity of an enzyme called beta-hexosaminidase A that catalyses the biodegradation of acidic fatty materials known as gangliosides. Gangliosides are made and biodegraded rapidly in early life as the brain develops. The incidence of Tay–Sachs is particularly high among people of Eastern European and Ashkenazi Jewish descent. Presentation Infants with Tay–Sachs disease appear to develop normally for the first few months of life. Then, as nerve cells become distended with fatty material, a relentless deterioration of mental and physical abilities occurs: The child becomes blind, deaf and unable to swallow. Muscles begin to atrophy and paralysis sets in. Other neurological symptoms include dementia, seizures and an increased startle reflex to noise. A much rarer form of the disorder occurs in patients in their 20s and early 30s, and is characterised by an unsteady gait and progressive neurological deterioration. People with Tay–Sachs also have “cherry-red” spots in their eyes. Investigations and diagnosis Patients and carriers of Tay–Sachs disease can be identified by a simple blood test that measures betahexosaminidase A activity. Both parents must carry the mutated gene in order to have an affected child: In these instances, there is a 25% chance with each pregnancy that the child will be affected with Tay–Sachs disease. Prenatal diagnosis is available if desired.

Decreased Golgi stimulation
Decreased Golgi stimulation is incorrect. Golgi transport disorders are thought to be associated with hereditary autoimmune mediated lung disease and arthritis.

Increased permeability of the blood–brain barrier
Increased permeability of the blood–brain barrier is incorrect. Increased risk of inflammatory CNS disorders may be seen with underlying blood–brain barrier disorders.

Increased receptor-mediated endocytosis
Increased receptor-mediated endocytosis is incorrect. Dent’s disease, associated with nephrolithiasis, is an example of a disease associated with defective receptor-mediated endocytosis.

Increase synthesis in the endoplasmic reticulum.

stem: A 74-year-old man receives an aciclovir shingles treatment pack from his GP. He is a retired chemist and is interested in asking you about how aciclovir works. Which one of the following best describes the step required for aciclovir activation?
options: Conversion to diphosphate form by viral thymidine kinase
Conversion to triphosphate form by host cell kinases
explanation:
Conversion to triphosphate form by host cell kinases
Aciclovir is a guanine analogue pro-drug that is used primarily for the treatment of herpes zoster or simplex infection. The key step in making it an active drug is conversion into a triphosphate form by host cell kinases, which eventually allows it to incorporate into viral DNA resulting in chain termination. Viral DNA polymerase is then unable to function and replication of the herpes virus is terminated. Peak plasma concentration is reached 1–2 hours after oral administration of aciclovir. Aciclovir is fairly rapidly eliminated, which necessitates multiple daily dosing regimens. Intravenous aciclovir may be given for disseminated herpes infection or in immunocompromised individuals. In herpes simplex virus the viral thymidine kinase is responsible for phosphorylating acyclovir to its monophosphate form. After monophosphorylation the host cellular kinases convert the drug monophosphate to its triphosphate form, which then selectively inhibits the viral DNA polymerase activity.

Conversion to diphosphate form by viral thymidine kinase
Conversion to diphosphate form by viral thymidine kinase is incorrect. The triphosphate form of aciclovir is the active drug.

Metabolism by intracellular phosphatases
Metabolism by intracellular phosphatases is incorrect. It is the addition of phosphate to aciclovir rather than removal of it which converts the pro-drug to the active form.

Reverse transcriptase activation
Reverse transcriptase activation is incorrect. Reverse transcriptase has no role in aciclovir Chat activation, butTutor reverse with AI transcriptase inhibitors are of course used in the treatment of HIV.

Viral protease activity.

stem: You are asked to help identify whether the child of a woman with a neuromuscular disorder is affected by the condition. A specific DNA sequence associated with the mutation which causes the disorder has been identified. Which one of the following methods can be used to identify a particular DNA sequence?
explanation:
Southern blotting
Southern blotting is a technique developed by Edwin Southern, a British biologist. It combines agarose gel electrophoresis for size separation of DNA with use of a filter membrane for probe hybridization. In reality PCR is more cost and resource effective with respect to mainstream testing for DNA sequences.

Eastern blotting
Eastern blotting is incorrect. Eastern blotting is used to describe post-translational modifications of proteins.

Northern blotting
Northern blotting is incorrect. Northern blotting is a technique used to identify RNA expression.

Southwestern blotting
Southwestern blotting is incorrect. Southwestern blotting is used to describe/study DNA-binding proteins.

Western blotting.

stem: You are consulting a 19-year-old man, who is thought to have a single gene congenital neurological degenerative disorder associated with progressive ataxia, for collection of genetic material. Concerning the identification of that gene, which one of the following statements is true?
options: 95% of possible human gene polymorphisms have already been identified
Neurological disorders can always be identified using a library of mutations associated with
RT-PCR is an evaluation method of choice
TP-PCR is an evaluation method of choice
Western blotting is a key step in work-up of the condition
explanation:
TP-PCR is an evaluation method of choice
Triple repeat primed PCR is useful in the evaluation of Friedreich’s ataxia, the most likely underlying diagnosis here. It has also been used in the evaluation of a number of other trinucleotide repeat disorders.

95% of possible human gene polymorphisms have already been identified
95% of possible human gene polymorphisms have already been identified is incorrect. 99% of the gene containing part of the human DNA sequence has been examined in the human genome project, with 15,000 full length human cDNAs identified.

Neurological disorders can always be identified using a library of mutations associated with
Neurological disorders can always be identified using a library of mutations associated with neurological disease Neurological disorders can always be identified using a library of mutations associated with neurological disease is incorrect. In some cases the specific DNA sequence for amplification may not yet have been identified.

RT-PCR is an evaluation method of choice
RT-PCR is an evaluation method of choice is incorrect. RT-PCR is used to identify specific sequences of RNA.

Western blotting is a key step in work-up of the condition.

stem: You are considering using a TNF-α antagonist in the treatment of a 45-year-old man with severe psoriasis. The patient wants to know more about this treatment and how it works. Which cells are mainly responsible for production of TNF-α?
explanation:
Macrophages
TNF-α is a cytokine involved in inflammation and the acute phase response. It is produced in a very wide range of cells across the immune system, but in large part by macrophages. Other cells that produce TNF-α exist in the neuronal system and in adipose tissue. Anti-TNF agents are used in the therapy of rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and seronegative arthritides and inflammatory bowel disease. Use of anti-TNF may be associated with reactivation of tuberculosis and viral hepatitis.

Eosinophils
Eosinophils is incorrect. Eosinophils produce a range of cytokines including IL-1, IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-8, IL-13, and TNF alpha, but most of the total TNF-α produced comes from macrophages.

Mast cells
Mast cells of Mast cells is incorrect. Mast cells predominantly release histamine, IL-4, IL-5, TGF-β and smaller amounts TNF-α versus macrophages.

Regulatory B lymphocytes
Regulatory B lymphocytes is incorrect. Regulatory B lymphocytes are recognised to secrete IL-10 or TGF-β1.

T-helper lymphocytes.

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents to the clinic with a mass in her right breast. It has been present for the past 2 months and has enlarged. She is extremely worried as her two sisters died of breast cancer a few years earlier. She undergoes genetic testing and is found to have a mutation in the BRCA1 gene. Which one of the following best describes the function of BRCA1?
explanation:
DNA repair
BRCA1 is important in the repair of double-stranded breaks in DNA. The process in which it participates is known as homologous replication, using the sister chromatid or homologous chromosome (or the same chromosome), depending on the cell cycle, to act as a template for repair. In patients who carry the BRCA1 mutation, these breaks in DNA accumulate, increasing the chance of malignancy. People with this mutation have around a 60% chance of developing breast cancer, and a 55% chance of developing ovarian cancer by the time they reach old age.

Apoptosis
Apoptosis is incorrect. Defective apoptosis is present in patients with p53 mutations, and leads to increased risk of a number of cancers. Li–Fraumeni syndrome is an example of a p53-dependent familial cancer syndrome.

DNA replication
DNA replication is incorrect. DNA polymerase mutations are associated with a number of cancers, including increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Growth repair
Growth repair is incorrect. Growth repair gene mutations are recognised to be associated with increased risk of colorectal cancer.

It freezes the cell cycle.

stem: A 17-year-old man is diagnosed with an abnormality of oligopeptide disposal. Which one of the following intracellular organelles is associated with the metabolism of oligopeptides?
explanation:
Lysosomes
Lysosomes are membrane-enclosed organelles that contain an array of enzymes capable of breaking down all types of biological polymers including peptides, nucleic acids, carbohydrates and lipids. Lysosomal storage diseases are a heritable group of human disorders characterised by the accumulation of undigested macromolecules within the lysosomes themselves, resulting in an increase in the size and number of these organelles and ultimately in cellular dysfunction and clinical abnormalities.

Golgi apparatus
Golgi apparatus is incorrect. The Golgi apparatus is responsible for post-translational modification of proteins.

Peroxisomes
Peroxisomes is incorrect. Peroxisomes are responsible for the breakdown of long-chain fatty acids so that they can be metabolised by mitochondria to provide energy.

Ribosomes
Ribosomes is incorrect. Ribosomes are responsible for protein manufacture rather than peptide disposal.

Smooth endoplasmic reticulum.

stem: DNA splicing is used in a number of areas of genetic engineering. Which of the following is the correct explanation of DNA splicing?
explanation:
Excision of introns
DNA splicing is the process of excision of introns and the joining together of exons which ultimately results in production of a peptide. Splicing has been used to genetically modify bacteria and yeasts to produce human peptides such as insulin and growth hormone. It is also the target of attempts at gene therapy to drive overexpression of therapeutic peptides or downregulate abnormal cellular processes.

Introduction of additional introns
Introduction of additional introns is incorrect. As introns are sequences of DNA which are not part of the final RNA sequence, it is exons which are the target for DNA splicing.

Introduction of peptide material
Introduction of peptide material is incorrect. Peptides are used as biological therapeutics, but do not have a role in DNA splicing.

Introduction of RNA
Introduction of RNA is incorrect. Both silencing RNAs and RNAs which drive protein expression are under development as therapeutics, but RNA introduction is not a feature of DNA splicing.

Promotion of transcription.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presented with progressive weight gain over a 2 year period. She had HIV and was taking stavudine, didanosine and indinavir. On examination she had a dorsocervical fat pad and central adiposity. She was diagnosed with lipodystrophy related to her HIV medication. She was given the opportunity to take part in an open label trial using leptin therapy. Which of the following is an action of leptin?
options: Stimulation of gonadotrophin releasing hormone secretion by the hypothalamus
Stimulation of hunger through actions at the hypothalamus
explanation:
Stimulation of gonadotrophin releasing hormone secretion by the hypothalamus
The main function of leptin is to stimulate a sense of satiety at the level of the hypothalamus, however one of its other effects is to stimulate the release of gonadotrophin releasing hormone. In turn this stimulates the release of luteinising hormone and follicle stimulating hormone from the anterior pituitary gland.

Inhibition of pubertal development
Inhibition of pubertal development is incorrect. Leptin is implicated in the onset of puberty alongside kisspeptin, hence the high incidence of early menarche in obese women. The effect of leptin on puberty takes place at the level of the hypothalamus, though its exact actions are not yet defined. The key role of leptin is to stimulate a sense of satiety through actions at the hypothalamus. However, it also stimulates the release of gonadotropin releasing hormone from the hypothalamus although levels of leptin outside the normal range may adversely affect fertility.

Reduction in cortical bone density
Reduction in cortical bone density is incorrect. In fact leptin has a role in bone remodelling, but while it decreases cancellous bone formation, it stimulates the production of cortical bone. It is thought that this is a mechanism to adapt the skeleton to increasing weight, as leptin levels are higher in obese individuals. Further to its role in bone metabolism, leptin has other peripheral and central effects. Its key role is to stimulate the sensation of satiety through actions at the hypothalamus, but it also stimulates the release of gonadotrophin releasing hormone from the hypothalamus.

Slowing of gastric emptying
Slowing of gastric emptying is incorrect. Slowing of gastric emptying is one of the effects of amylin, another hormone involved in the feeling of satiety (the key function of leptin). Leptin does not have any effects on gastric emptying; it stimulates satiety through effects on the hypothalamus. It has a number of other effects on the hypothalamus, including stimulating the secretion of gonadotrophin releasing hormone.

Stimulation of hunger through actions at the hypothalamus.

stem: You are asked to review a 17-year-old who suffers from leprechaunism (Donohue Syndrome). You understand that this occurs as a result of a mutation associated with the insulin receptor. Where is the insulin receptor located?
explanation:
Cell membrane
The insulin receptor is a transmembrane receptor which belongs to the tyrosine kinase family of receptors that are involved in intracellular signalling by phosphorylation of intracellular proteins. These proteins include IRS-1, whose effects include upregulation of the GLUT-4 glucose transporter, which is responsible for facilitating glucose entry into the cell. Leprechaunism (Donohue Syndrome) is an autosomal recessive condition that results from a mutation that leads to non-functioning insulin receptors.

Chromatin
Chromatin is incorrect. Chromatin is not a target for insulin as it is intracellular.

Cytoplasm
Cytoplasm is incorrect. The cytoplasm contains a number of second messengers; activity of some is upregulated by binding of insulin to its receptor, but the insulin receptor itself is not found within the cytoplasm.

Endoplasmic reticulum
Endoplasmic reticulum is incorrect. The endoplasmic reticulum is responsible for protein synthesis and does not possess insulin receptors.

Nucleus/nuclear membrane.
